transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it’s nice to meet you too, doctor. I, um, I guess I made this appointment because I just... I feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It’s the most frustrating thing, and honestly, it’s just exhausting. You know, at my age—I'm 66 now, and I haven't been working for a while, so my days are my own—you’d think I would just be taking it easy. My sister is always telling me to just sit down and enjoy my time. 

But I sit down in my recliner in the living room, and it’s like... it's like I have to jump up and do the next thing. Immediately. Even when I don't actually have anything pressing to do! I'll just be sitting there, trying to watch a program, and I get this feeling like I need to be moving, so I get up and start wiping down the counters or reorganizing the hall closet for the third time this month. And the worst part is, I’ll be completely worn out. I mean, my body is just bone-tired, my knees ache, and I really, truly should be sitting still and resting. But I just can't. The second I try to relax, that feeling creeps right back up my arms and legs, and I'm back on my feet before I even realize I've stood up. It's just... it's driving me a little crazy, to be honest with you, because I just want to be able to sit in my own house without feeling like a wound-up toy.
When you’re resting or sitting still, does the urge to move get noticeably worse?

Oh, absolutely. That’s—well, like I was just saying a minute ago, that is exactly when it hits me the hardest. When I’m up and puttering around, sweeping the kitchen or walking down to get the mail, I don't notice it as much. But the very second my bottom hits that recliner cushion... oh my goodness. It’s like my whole body just rejects the idea of resting. 

I’ll sit there, and I try, I really do try to just be still. I'll tell myself to just watch my shows, because I am just so worn out and I know I really should be sitting still. My knees are practically begging me to stay put! But then... it’s just like I said, I feel like I absolutely cannot settle inside my own skin. It actually gets so much worse when I try to relax. It starts to feel almost unbearable, like this awful buzzing in my legs, and the longer I force myself to stay in the chair, the louder that feeling gets. 

Even though I am completely exhausted, it just builds and builds until I feel like I have to jump up and do the next thing. And the silly part is, there usually isn't even a 'next thing' to do! I’ll just invent something, like rearranging the coasters or checking the locks on the back door for the second time, because sitting still actually feels worse than being tired on my feet. It’s just so backward, isn't it? You'd think resting would feel good when you're my age and you're tired, but for me, trying to sit still is just pure torture.
When you get up and move around, does that uncomfortable feeling go away, even briefly?

Well, I guess... I mean, yes and no? It’s hard to explain. When I finally give in and just stand up—like when I was talking about checking the locks on the back door or wiping the counters—the awful buzzing feeling does let up a little bit. It’s like letting the steam out of a kettle, I suppose. For those few minutes I’m moving, I’m not crawling out of my skin in the exact same way. 

But the problem is, it doesn't really *go away*, you know? It’s more like I’m just distracting myself from it by being busy. And then, because I’m so exhausted and my knees are aching like I mentioned, I eventually have to sit back down. And the very second I do—boom. It’s right back. It’s almost like the feeling was just waiting for me to sit down again so it could start all over. 

So, I’ll be up and down, up and down, all evening. Last Tuesday, for example, I must have gotten up from my chair during *Jeopardy!* at least four times. I went to the kitchen, I watered a plant that didn't even need watering, I adjusted the blinds... and every time I was up, I felt a tiny bit of relief from that terrible restless feeling, but I was so tired! And then I’d sit back down for Final Jeopardy, and the buzzing would start all over again before the commercial break even finished. It’s just this endless, exhausting cycle, and moving only gives me the tiniest little break before it all starts up again. It’s not a real fix at all.
Is this restless, buzzing feeling usually worse in the evening or at night?

Well, I... I don't really know if it's worse at any particular time of day, to be perfectly honest with you. It's just... it's just always there whenever I try to sit down. I mean, evening, morning, middle of the afternoon—it doesn't seem to care what time the clock says. 

Like yesterday, for instance. It was maybe 10:30 in the morning, right after I finished my coffee. I thought, "I'll just sit here at the kitchen table and read the paper." My sister gets the paper delivered, and she always saves the crossword for me, which is so sweet of her, really. So I sat down with my pen, feeling perfectly fine, and I hadn't even gotten through the across clues before that buzzing started up in my legs. Broad daylight! And then, of course, the same thing happened after dinner when I tried to watch the news. So, no, I can't say it's an evening thing. It just seems to be a "whenever I try to rest" thing, which is just... well, it's just so frustrating, because a person my age should be able to sit and read the paper at 10:30 in the morning without feeling like they've got electricity running through their veins, shouldn't they? It just doesn't seem to matter what time it is, the feeling is exactly the same.
Is that buzzing, restless feeling mainly in your legs?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've thought about it quite a bit. I mean, my sister asked me the same thing just the other day when I was pacing around her living room during our weekly canasta game. She said, "Is it just your legs?" And I really had to stop and think about it. 

I suppose the legs are where I notice it the most, especially when I'm sitting in my recliner. It’s like my knees and my calves are just full of this... this nervous energy. But then, if I'm being completely honest, it's not *just* my legs. It’s almost like my whole body gets in on the act. My hands start fidgeting, I'll start picking at my fingernails, or I’ll catch myself tapping my fingers on the armrest. Sometimes I even feel it in my chest, just this tightness, this... this overwhelming urge that I just have to move *something*. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to sit through church, and Pastor Miller was giving a lovely sermon, really he was, but I just couldn't keep still. My legs were bouncing, yes, but I was also shifting my weight, adjusting my scarf, looking around... it was like every part of me was just refusing to settle down. So, while I do feel that awful buzzing most strongly in my legs, it really feels like it takes over my entire body when it gets bad. It’s like my whole self is just allergic to sitting still, if that makes any sense at all.
Have you been feeling unusually upbeat or euphoric lately?

Upbeat? Oh, goodness, no. Heavens, no. I mean... I don't think I've felt anything close to euphoric in... well, I couldn't even tell you how long. It's actually quite the opposite, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I mean, how could a person possibly feel upbeat when they're constantly jumping out of their own skin, you know? 

My sister—the one I play canasta with—she actually said to me just the other day, she said, "You seem so cranky lately." And I told her, I said, "I'm not trying to be cranky, I'm just worn to the absolute bone!" Because really, this whole inability to just sit and relax, it takes every ounce of joy out of my day. I used to love just sitting quietly on the porch with a cup of tea, watching the neighborhood go by, but now it's just a chore to even try. 

So, no, definitely not upbeat. If anything, I'm just... I'm just so terribly frustrated and tired all the time. Euphoria is the absolute last word I would use to describe how I've been feeling. I mean, I try to keep a positive attitude, I really do, because my mother always taught me that nobody likes a sourpuss, but it's hard. It's just very, very hard to put on a happy face when your body won't let you rest for even five minutes. So, no, doctor, no euphoria here. Just a lot of pacing and sighing, I'm afraid.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason to worry?

Worrying? Well, I... I don't think so. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier, not in the grand scheme of things. Of course, everyone worries a little bit, don't they? You worry if you left the stove on, or if the mail carrier is going to bend the magazines you ordered, or... or if it's going to rain when you've just hung the laundry out. But that's just normal, everyday stuff. 

My mother, now she was a worrier. She would fret over every little thing until she made herself sick. She used to sit at the kitchen table and just wring her hands about the weather, the neighbors, the price of eggs... you name it, she worried about it. But I've never really been like that. I don't sit around chewing my fingernails about things that haven't happened yet, or things I can't control. 

My problem isn't that my mind is racing with all these terrible thoughts about what could go wrong. It's just... it's just this physical inability to be still. Like I was saying about the church service, I wasn't sitting there worrying about anything in particular. I wasn't fretting over the sermon or thinking about what I was going to make for Sunday dinner. My mind was perfectly calm, but my body just wouldn't cooperate. So, no, I don't find myself worrying for no reason. It's really just the restlessness that's driving me up the wall, not my thoughts. I just wish I could get my body to be as quiet as my mind is most of the time.
Have you started or changed any medications around the time this restlessness began?

Medications? Oh, let me think about that for a second... I mean, I take my usual things, of course. Dr. Evans—he's my primary care doctor, just a lovely man, always asks about my sister when I go in—he has me on a little pink pill for my blood pressure, and I take a daily vitamin. One of those ones for women over fifty, though I suppose I'm well past fifty now! But I've been taking those for years and years. Oh, and a calcium supplement, because you know at my age you really have to watch out for your bones. My Aunt Mildred broke her hip just stepping off a curb at the grocery store, and I certainly don't want to go through that. 

But as for anything new? Or changing my doses? No, no, absolutely not. I keep all my pill bottles lined up on the lazy Susan in the kitchen cabinet, right next to the salt and pepper shakers, and it's been the exact same lineup for as long as I can remember. I haven't added anything new, and Dr. Evans hasn't changed my prescriptions at all. I go to the pharmacy down on Elm Street—the one with the nice young pharmacist, David, I think his name is, or maybe Daniel—and it's always just my usual refills every month like clockwork. 

So, no, nothing like that. I haven't taken a single new pill or changed anything that could have brought on all this awful pacing and fidgeting. I haven't even taken so much as a new brand of cough syrup. It just sort of... well, it's just been happening, without me changing a single thing in my routine.
When you’re sitting still, do you feel an uncomfortable sensation in your legs that makes you want to move them?

An uncomfortable sensation? Like a tingling or a pain or something? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like my legs are aching or feeling funny. You know, I read an article in Reader's Digest just a few months ago—or maybe it was last year, I was at the dentist's office waiting for my cleaning, Dr. Miller is always running a little behind—and it was talking about people who get these creepy-crawly feelings in their legs at night. Like bugs are under their skin! Good heavens, just the thought of it gave me the absolute shivers. But no, I don't have anything like that. My legs feel perfectly fine, physically speaking. 

It's not that my legs are uncomfortable, it's just that I... well, I just can't keep them still. Or my hands, or any of me, really. When I sit down in my floral armchair in the evenings to watch Jeopardy—Alex Trebek, God rest his soul, I still miss him, though that new fellow is certainly doing his best—I sit there and my legs don't hurt, but I just have to bounce my knee. Or I have to stand up and go check if I locked the back door, or I get up to straighten the doilies on the end tables. 

It's not a localized feeling in my legs telling me to move because they feel bad or strange. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be doing something, moving somehow, like my motor is just running and running. My sister actually asked me the same thing, she said, "Are your joints bothering you?" because she has terribly bad arthritis in her knees, poor thing. But I told her, no, it's not a physical discomfort in the legs themselves. Just this awful, exhausting urge to keep moving. So, no, no weird sensations like that.
When this happens, do you feel an inner sense of restlessness or tension, like you just cannot stay still?

Yes! Oh, yes, that is exactly it. That’s the perfect way to describe it. In fact, that's... well, to be completely honest with you, Doctor, that is the main reason I finally made the appointment to come in. I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. 

It's the strangest, most frustrating thing in the world. I'll be absolutely exhausted, just worn down to the bone—you know how it is when you've been going all day, maybe I've been dusting the baseboards or sweeping the front porch, which I try to do every Tuesday, though lately the wind has been blowing so much dirt back up it hardly seems worth the effort. But anyway, I'll think to myself, 'It's time to sit down and rest.' I *should* be sitting still. I really want to just sit there and relax. 

But there's this... this awful tension inside me. And before I even realize what I'm doing, I just have to jump up and do the next thing. I'll be completely worn out, my energy completely spent, but I'll pop right out of my chair because I suddenly feel like I absolutely must go reorganize the Tupperware cabinet or check if the laundry is dry. It’s like I’m a wind-up toy that somebody wound up way too tight, and even when the spring should be completely unwound, I just can't stop. It's exhausting, it really is, never being able to just exist quietly in your own body.
Do you often feel keyed up or on edge?

Keyed up? On edge? Well... I don't know if I'd use those exact words. It's not like I'm sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Like I'm not... I'm not nervous about something specific happening. My neighbor, Betty—she lives in the blue house next door, the one with the lovely hydrangeas, though she really needs to prune them back this year—she's always on edge. She's terrified of burglars, absolutely convinced someone is going to break in, so she's always jumping at every little noise. 

I'm not like that. I'm not anxious or fearful or keyed up in that way. It's just that physical restlessness I was telling you about. It's just my body that won't settle down, not my mind worrying over things. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel on edge, not like I'm startled or tense about something bad happening. It's just that constant, exhausting need to be moving, like my motor is stuck on high, even when my brain is perfectly calm and just wants to watch Jeopardy in peace.
Do you spend a lot of time feeling anxious about several different parts of your life?

Anxious about lots of different parts of my life? Oh, no, no, not at all. Like I was just saying with Betty and her burglar fears—I'm really not a worrier. I don't sit around fretting about my finances or my health or whether the roof is going to leak if we get a heavy rain, though we certainly need the rain, my garden is just parched right now. The tomatoes are looking terribly sad, just drooping over their cages. 

But no, I don't spend my time feeling anxious about things. I mean, everyone has little concerns now and then, of course. When my grandson was applying to colleges last year, I hoped he'd get into a good one—and he did, he's at the state university now, doing wonderfully, studying business or maybe communications, I can never keep it straight. But I wasn't losing sleep over it. I don't have this dark cloud of anxiety hanging over me about my daily life. It really is just that physical inability to sit still, that buzzing feeling in my body. My mind is actually quite peaceful, most of the time! I'm perfectly content with my life, I just wish I could sit still long enough to enjoy it without feeling like I need to jump up and scrub the kitchen sink for the third time in a day. So, no, anxiety isn't a problem for me at all.
When you feel this need to keep moving, do you feel anxious?

Well, no, like I was just trying to explain... I really don't. I know it probably looks like I'm anxious to anyone watching me, though. My husband, bless his heart—before he passed, God rest his soul—he used to say to me, he'd say, 'What on earth has got you so worked up?' because I'd be pacing the living room floor right in the middle of Wheel of Fortune. We never missed an episode of Wheel, you know, we watched it every single evening after dinner. 

But I wasn't worked up at all! I wasn't worrying about the electric bill or whether the car needed new tires or anything like that. My mind was perfectly calm, just trying to guess the puzzle. It’s just... my legs just needed to go. So when I get that sudden urge to jump up and start moving, there is absolutely no worry attached to it. None whatsoever. It's strictly a physical drive. 

It's almost like... well, like a sneeze! You don't feel anxious when you feel a sneeze coming on, do you? You just feel that tickle, that build-up in your nose, and you absolutely have to let it out, you can't just hold it in. That's exactly what my body is doing when I get that restless feeling. It's just a physical pressure that needs a release, just... with pacing around the kitchen island or wiping down the countertops instead of sneezing. So no, no anxiety at all when it happens. Just the moving.

It’s like my whole self is just allergic to sitting still, if that makes any sense at all.

inference.note: Restlessness is not predominantly leg-limited and lacks evening/night predominance, which argues against classic G25.81 but does not exclude it entirely. Generalized/internal restlessness and whole-body fidgeting keep anxiety-spectrum and mood causes in the differential.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is driven by an abnormally elevated or expansive mood, which would help distinguish mania/hypomania from anxiety or restless legs.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually upbeat or euphoric lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling unusually upbeat or euphoric, which are symptoms of mania. My symptom profile does not include mania or euphoria.

patient.answer:
Upbeat? Oh, goodness, no. Heavens, no. I mean... I don't think I've felt anything close to euphoric in... well, I couldn't even tell you how long. It's actually quite the opposite, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I mean, how could a person possibly feel upbeat when they're constantly jumping out of their own skin, you know? 

My sister—the one I play canasta with—she actually said to me just the other day, she said, "You seem so cranky lately." And I told her, I said, "I'm not trying to be cranky, I'm just worn to the absolute bone!" Because really, this whole inability to just sit and relax, it takes every ounce of joy out of my day. I used to love just sitting quietly on the porch with a cup of tea, watching the neighborhood go by, but now it's just a chore to even try. 

So, no, definitely not upbeat. If anything, I'm just... I'm just so terribly frustrated and tired all the time. Euphoria is the absolute last word I would use to describe how I've been feeling. I mean, I try to keep a positive attitude, I really do, because my mother always taught me that nobody likes a sourpuss, but it's hard. It's just very, very hard to put on a happy face when your body won't let you rest for even five minutes. So, no, doctor, no euphoria here. Just a lot of pacing and sighing, I'm afraid.

inference.note: Denied euphoria/unusually upbeat mood, making F30.9 and F31.9 less likely. Persistent whole-body restlessness still leaves anxiety disorders in the differential, though features remain strongly suggestive of G25.81-like restlessness.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is accompanied by excessive, hard-to-control worry, which would help distinguish generalized anxiety from akathisia/restless legs.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason to worry?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry or anxiety, which is not part of the patient's ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worrying? Well, I... I don't think so. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier, not in the grand scheme of things. Of course, everyone worries a little bit, don't they? You worry if you left the stove on, or if the mail carrier is going to bend the magazines you ordered, or... or if it's going to rain when you've just hung the laundry out. But that's just normal, everyday stuff. 

My mother, now she was a worrier. She would fret over every little thing until she made herself sick. She used to sit at the kitchen table and just wring her hands about the weather, the neighbors, the price of eggs... you name it, she worried about it. But I've never really been like that. I don't sit around chewing my fingernails about things that haven't happened yet, or things I can't control. 

My problem isn't that my mind is racing with all these terrible thoughts about what could go wrong. It's just... it's just this physical inability to be still. Like I was saying about the church service, I wasn't sitting there worrying about anything in particular. I wasn't fretting over the sermon or thinking about what I was going to make for Sunday dinner. My mind was perfectly calm, but my body just wouldn't cooperate. So, no, I don't find myself worrying for no reason. It's really just the restlessness that's driving me up the wall, not my thoughts. I just wish I could get my body to be as quiet as my mind is most of the time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is associated with a medication-induced akathisia picture rather than generalized anxiety or restless legs syndrome.
doctor.question: Have you started or changed any medications around the time this restlessness began?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medication changes to rule out medication-induced restlessness (like akathisia), which is not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Medications? Oh, let me think about that for a second... I mean, I take my usual things, of course. Dr. Evans—he's my primary care doctor, just a lovely man, always asks about my sister when I go in—he has me on a little pink pill for my blood pressure, and I take a daily vitamin. One of those ones for women over fifty, though I suppose I'm well past fifty now! But I've been taking those for years and years. Oh, and a calcium supplement, because you know at my age you really have to watch out for your bones. My Aunt Mildred broke her hip just stepping off a curb at the grocery store, and I certainly don't want to go through that. 

But as for anything new? Or changing my doses? No, no, absolutely not. I keep all my pill bottles lined up on the lazy Susan in the kitchen cabinet, right next to the salt and pepper shakers, and it's been the exact same lineup for as long as I can remember. I haven't added anything new, and Dr. Evans hasn't changed my prescriptions at all. I go to the pharmacy down on Elm Street—the one with the nice young pharmacist, David, I think his name is, or maybe Daniel—and it's always just my usual refills every month like clockwork. 

So, no, nothing like that. I haven't taken a single new pill or changed anything that could have brought on all this awful pacing and fidgeting. I haven't even taken so much as a new brand of cough syrup. It just sort of... well, it's just been happening, without me changing a single thing in my routine.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is driven by an unpleasant internal sensation in the legs that creates an urge to move, which would support restless legs syndrome over anxiety.
doctor.question: When you’re sitting still, do you feel an uncomfortable sensation in your legs that makes you want to move them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about an uncomfortable sensation in the legs that creates an urge to move, which is a screening question for Restless Legs Syndrome, not covered by the ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
An uncomfortable sensation? Like a tingling or a pain or something? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like my legs are aching or feeling funny. You know, I read an article in Reader's Digest just a few months ago—or maybe it was last year, I was at the dentist's office waiting for my cleaning, Dr. Miller is always running a little behind—and it was talking about people who get these creepy-crawly feelings in their legs at night. Like bugs are under their skin! Good heavens, just the thought of it gave me the absolute shivers. But no, I don't have anything like that. My legs feel perfectly fine, physically speaking. 

It's not that my legs are uncomfortable, it's just that I... well, I just can't keep them still. Or my hands, or any of me, really. When I sit down in my floral armchair in the evenings to watch Jeopardy—Alex Trebek, God rest his soul, I still miss him, though that new fellow is certainly doing his best—I sit there and my legs don't hurt, but I just have to bounce my knee. Or I have to stand up and go check if I locked the back door, or I get up to straighten the doilies on the end tables. 

It's not a localized feeling in my legs telling me to move because they feel bad or strange. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be doing something, moving somehow, like my motor is just running and running. My sister actually asked me the same thing, she said, "Are your joints bothering you?" because she has terribly bad arthritis in her knees, poor thing. But I told her, no, it's not a physical discomfort in the legs themselves. Just this awful, exhausting urge to keep moving. So, no, no weird sensations like that.

inference.note: Ruled out G25.81: patient denies uncomfortable leg sensations and denies evening/night predominance; restlessness is generalized rather than leg-focused. Remaining possibilities are anxiety-spectrum disorders with prominent psychomotor restlessness.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is driven by subjective inner tension with inability to remain still, which would support akathisia over generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: When this happens, do you feel an inner sense of restlessness or tension, like you just cannot stay still?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore, like I have to jump up and do the next thing even when I am worn out and should be sitting still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about an inner sense of restlessness and the inability to stay still, which directly maps to the symptom of feeling restless.

patient.answer:
Yes! Oh, yes, that is exactly it. That’s the perfect way to describe it. In fact, that's... well, to be completely honest with you, Doctor, that is the main reason I finally made the appointment to come in. I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. 

It's the strangest, most frustrating thing in the world. I'll be absolutely exhausted, just worn down to the bone—you know how it is when you've been going all day, maybe I've been dusting the baseboards or sweeping the front porch, which I try to do every Tuesday, though lately the wind has been blowing so much dirt back up it hardly seems worth the effort. But anyway, I'll think to myself, 'It's time to sit down and rest.' I *should* be sitting still. I really want to just sit there and relax. 

But there's this... this awful tension inside me. And before I even realize what I'm doing, I just have to jump up and do the next thing. I'll be completely worn out, my energy completely spent, but I'll pop right out of my chair because I suddenly feel like I absolutely must go reorganize the Tupperware cabinet or check if the laundry is dry. It’s like I’m a wind-up toy that somebody wound up way too tight, and even when the spring should be completely unwound, I just can't stop. It's exhausting, it really is, never being able to just exist quietly in your own body.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is accompanied by generalized autonomic anxiety symptoms, which would support generalized anxiety disorder over unspecified anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Do you often feel keyed up or on edge?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling 'keyed up or on edge', which is a symptom of Generalized Anxiety Disorder. While the patient experiences restlessness (which was addressed in the previous question), 'keyed up or on edge' as a distinct anxiety symptom is not part of the provided ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Keyed up? On edge? Well... I don't know if I'd use those exact words. It's not like I'm sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Like I'm not... I'm not nervous about something specific happening. My neighbor, Betty—she lives in the blue house next door, the one with the lovely hydrangeas, though she really needs to prune them back this year—she's always on edge. She's terrified of burglars, absolutely convinced someone is going to break in, so she's always jumping at every little noise. 

I'm not like that. I'm not anxious or fearful or keyed up in that way. It's just that physical restlessness I was telling you about. It's just my body that won't settle down, not my mind worrying over things. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel on edge, not like I'm startled or tense about something bad happening. It's just that constant, exhausting need to be moving, like my motor is stuck on high, even when my brain is perfectly calm and just wants to watch Jeopardy in peace.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is driven by anxiety about multiple life areas, which would support generalized anxiety disorder over unspecified anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Do you spend a lot of time feeling anxious about several different parts of your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about generalized anxiety and excessive worry across multiple areas of life, which is not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Anxious about lots of different parts of my life? Oh, no, no, not at all. Like I was just saying with Betty and her burglar fears—I'm really not a worrier. I don't sit around fretting about my finances or my health or whether the roof is going to leak if we get a heavy rain, though we certainly need the rain, my garden is just parched right now. The tomatoes are looking terribly sad, just drooping over their cages. 

But no, I don't spend my time feeling anxious about things. I mean, everyone has little concerns now and then, of course. When my grandson was applying to colleges last year, I hoped he'd get into a good one—and he did, he's at the state university now, doing wonderfully, studying business or maybe communications, I can never keep it straight. But I wasn't losing sleep over it. I don't have this dark cloud of anxiety hanging over me about my daily life. It really is just that physical inability to sit still, that buzzing feeling in my body. My mind is actually quite peaceful, most of the time! I'm perfectly content with my life, I just wish I could sit still long enough to enjoy it without feeling like I need to jump up and scrub the kitchen sink for the third time in a day. So, no, anxiety isn't a problem for me at all.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the restlessness is anxiety-driven despite the patient's denial, to distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from unspecified anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: When you feel this need to keep moving, do you feel anxious?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the restlessness is accompanied by anxiety, which is a question to rule out an anxiety disorder. My symptom profile for ADHD does not include anxiety symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, no, like I was just trying to explain... I really don't. I know it probably looks like I'm anxious to anyone watching me, though. My husband, bless his heart—before he passed, God rest his soul—he used to say to me, he'd say, 'What on earth has got you so worked up?' because I'd be pacing the living room floor right in the middle of Wheel of Fortune. We never missed an episode of Wheel, you know, we watched it every single evening after dinner. 

But I wasn't worked up at all! I wasn't worrying about the electric bill or whether the car needed new tires or anything like that. My mind was perfectly calm, just trying to guess the puzzle. It’s just... my legs just needed to go. So when I get that sudden urge to jump up and start moving, there is absolutely no worry attached to it. None whatsoever. It's strictly a physical drive. 

It's almost like... well, like a sneeze! You don't feel anxious when you feel a sneeze coming on, do you? You just feel that tickle, that build-up in your nose, and you absolutely have to let it out, you can't just hold it in. That's exactly what my body is doing when I get that restless feeling. It's just a physical pressure that needs a release, just... with pacing around the kitchen island or wiping down the countertops instead of sneezing. So no, no anxiety at all when it happens. Just the moving.

inference.note: Ruled out generalized/unspecified anxiety by repeated denial of excessive worry, anxious affect, or feeling keyed up; symptoms are a non-volitional inner restlessness with inability to remain seated, worse at rest and relieved by movement, without leg dysesthesias or evening predominance, making anxiety less likely and pointing to a movement-related/restlessness presentation best captured here as F45.8.
